In truth. Chevron's justifying presumption is, as Members of this 
Court have often recognized, a fiction. So we have spent the better part of 
four decades imposing one limitation on Chevron after another, pruning its 
presumption on the understanding that “where it is in doubt that Congress 
actually intended to delegate particular interpretive authority to an 
agency. Chevron is mapplicable.’ ”
Consider the many refinements we have made in an effort to match 
Chevron's presumption to reahty. We have said that Chevron applies only 
when it appears that Congress delegated authority to the agency generally 
to make rules carrying the force of law, and that the agency interpretation 
claiming deference was promulgated in the exercise of that authority.” 
Mead, 533 U.S. at 226—227. In practice, that threshold requirement— 
sometimes called Chevron step zero”—^largely limits Chevron to “the fi’uits 
of notice-and-comment rulemaking or formal adjudication.” But even when 
those processes are used, deference is still not warranted “where the 
regulation is procedurally defective’—^that is, where the agency errs by 
failing to follow the correct procedures in issuing the regulation.”
Even where those procedural hurdles are cleared, substantive ones 
remain. Most notably. Chevron does not apply if the question at issue is 
one of “deep ‘economic and pohtical significance.’ ” King v. Burwell, 576 
U.S. 473, 486 (2015). * * * Nor have we applied Chevron to agency
